lead: Partial prestressing is a deliberate mix of prestressed tendons and ordinary reinforcing bars. The tendons apply compression and carry part of the bending moment; the bars carry the rest and control cracks. It exists because full prestressing can be costly and can make a member too cambered or brittle, while ordinary reinforced concrete needs larger sections and shows wider cracks under heavy load. You meet it in bridge decks, long-span floors, water tanks and precast panels where a small, controlled tension under service load is acceptable.
prereq: You need: 6.6; Unit 2 reinforced concrete flexure and serviceability.

blocks.text: A partially prestressed member has both prestressing steel (tendons) and non-prestressed reinforcement (ordinary bars). The two work together. Prestressing steel is high-tensile wire, strand or bar; ordinary steel is a ribbed bar such as Fe 415 or Fe 500. The tendons are tensioned to a force P, and the bars are placed like normal RC steel. Under service load the section may be uncracked, cracked, or on the point of cracking. A fully prestressed member is usually designed to keep concrete in compression or at zero tension. Ordinary RC has no prestress at all. Partial prestressing sits between them.

blocks.where: λ is the prestress contribution ratio; M<sub>p</sub> is the moment resisted by the prestress effect; M<sub>u</sub> is the total required moment. Some texts call this the degree of prestressing.

blocks.text: Full prestressing gives small deflection and no tension, but it needs a large force, many tendons and strong anchorages. The member may camber upward and have little ductility. Ordinary RC is simple and cheap but cracks and deflects. Partial prestressing uses tendons for a large share of the moment and bars for the peak and for crack control. It reduces the prestress force, the number of tendons, the camber and the end-block reinforcement. It is not a lower grade of full prestressing; it is a different design choice.
The spectrum runs from full prestressing with no tension, through partial prestressing with tendons plus rebar, to ordinary RC with no prestress. The figure shows this order.

The design idea is to split the required moment. Choose the tendon force and profile so prestress supplies M<sub>p</sub>, and let ordinary bars supply M<sub>s</sub>. A first estimate uses M<sub>u</sub> = M<sub>p</sub> + M<sub>s</sub>. Exact ultimate analysis uses strain compatibility because the tendon stress at failure is not simply its initial stress, and the two steel types may have different lever arms.

blocks.where: A<sub>s</sub> is the area of ordinary tension bars in mm²; M<sub>s</sub> is the moment carried by those bars in N mm; f<sub>y</sub> is the yield strength of the ordinary steel in N/mm²; z is the lever arm in mm.

items: For the service stress check, use the effective prestress after losses to find the service-load prestress moment.

For the ultimate-strength estimate, take the tendon stress at the ultimate limit state (or assume an ultimate tendon stress and confirm it by strain compatibility) and find the ultimate prestress moment M<sub>p</sub>.
Subtract this ultimate M<sub>p</sub> from the total factored moment to get M<sub>s</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> - M<sub>p</sub>; both terms must be at the same ultimate limit state.
Find the ordinary steel area from A<sub>s</sub> = M<sub>s</sub> / (0.87 f<sub>y</sub> z), then choose bars.
Check service stresses and crack width using the effective prestress after losses.
Check ultimate strength by strain compatibility, and check ductility and anchorage.

blocks.text: Both checks matter. A section can be strong at ultimate and still fail serviceability by wide cracks or excessive tension. A section can look safe at service and still be brittle at ultimate. Partial prestressing therefore needs the service stress check, the crack-width check and the ultimate strength check.

Partial prestressing is common where full prestressing is too expensive or too stiff. Examples are bridge decks, precast floor slabs, water tanks, piles and parking structures. In a long-span floor, tendons can carry the main moment and ordinary bars can handle peak moments near supports and control cracking. Fewer tendons mean fewer anchorages, less end-block reinforcement and simpler detailing. The builder can use conventional rebar skills for part of the steel.

Economy comes from balance, not from saving steel alone. The section must still satisfy service stress, crack width, ultimate strength and deflection. A cheap design that cracks badly will need repair, and a design with too much prestress may need extra camber control. The engineer chooses the prestress contribution ratio to suit span, load, crack limits and construction method.

figure.caption: The three levels from top to bottom: full prestressing with no tension, partial prestressing with tendons and ordinary bars, and ordinary reinforced concrete with no prestress. Notice that partial prestressing is a deliberate middle choice, not a weak copy of full prestressing.

spec.aria: A spectrum from full prestressing with no tension, through partial prestressing with tendons and ordinary bars, to ordinary reinforced concrete.

examples.question: A simply supported beam must resist a factored moment M<sub>u</sub> = 300 kN m. The design uses partial prestressing: prestress is taken to contribute M<sub>p</sub> = 180 kN m and ordinary Fe 415 bars carry the remaining M<sub>s</sub>. Take the lever arm for the ordinary bars as z = 600 mm and use 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> in the steel force. Find the area of ordinary tension reinforcement A<sub>s</sub>. State one serviceability check that must still be made.
steps: Remaining moment for ordinary bars: M<sub>s</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> - M<sub>p</sub> = 300 - 180 = 120 kN m.
Convert to N mm: M<sub>s</sub> = 120 × 10⁶ N mm.
A<sub>s</sub> = 553.9 mm², so provide about 554 mm²; for example, two 20 mm bars give 628 mm².
Serviceability check: check tensile stress and crack width under service load; also confirm ultimate strength by strain compatibility.
examples.answer: The ordinary tension reinforcement required is A<sub>s</sub> = 554 mm², and the member must still be checked for service tensile stress and crack width.
examples.check:
Mu = 300
Mp = 180
Ms = Mu - Mp
fy = 415
z = 600
As = Ms * 10**6 / (0.87 * fy * z)
print(round(As))

traps: Treating partial prestressing as a lower grade of full prestressing. It is a deliberate mix, and crack width and ultimate strength both need checks.
Adding the prestress moment and the rebar moment without checking strain compatibility. The tendon stress at ultimate is not simply the initial prestress, and the lever arms may differ.
Using the gross concrete section for service stresses after the section has cracked. A cracked transformed section is needed for realistic tension and crack checks.
Forgetting losses of prestress in the service check. The jacking force is not the effective force that remains.
Mixing units: kN m must become N mm before dividing by stresses in N/mm².

quiz.q: Define partial prestressing in one sentence.
quiz.a: Partial prestressing is a design in which prestressed tendons and ordinary reinforcing bars together resist the required moment and control service behaviour.

quiz.q: What does the prestress contribution ratio λ = M<sub>p</sub> / M<sub>u</sub> compare?
quiz.a: It compares the moment resisted by the prestress effect, M<sub>p</sub>, with the total required moment, M<sub>u</sub>.

quiz.q: Why are ordinary bars used in a partially prestressed member?
quiz.a: They carry part of the moment, control crack width after the concrete cracks, and add ductility and toughness.

quiz.q: Why is an ultimate strength check alone not enough for a partially prestressed beam?
quiz.a: The beam may be strong at ultimate but show excessive tensile stress or wide cracks under service load, so service stress and crack width must also be checked.

quiz.q: A beam has M<sub>u</sub> = 400 kN m. Prestress contributes M<sub>p</sub> = 250 kN m. Ordinary Fe 415 bars have lever arm z = 550 mm. Find A<sub>s</sub>.
quiz.a: M<sub>s</sub> = 400 - 250 = 150 kN m = 150 × 10⁶ N mm. A<sub>s</sub> = 150 × 10⁶ / (0.87 × 415 × 550) = 755 mm² approximately.

quiz.q: A partially prestressed floor slab shows wider cracks than allowed at service load, although its ultimate moment is sufficient. Suggest two design changes and state the effect of each.
quiz.a: Increase ordinary reinforcement to control crack width, or increase effective prestress within limits to reduce tensile stress. Either change must be rechecked for service stress, camber and ultimate ductility.

quiz.q: Compare full prestressing, partial prestressing and ordinary RC for crack control and ductility.
quiz.a: Full prestressing usually keeps concrete uncracked but can be brittle and costly. Partial prestressing allows controlled cracking, uses bars for ductility and crack control, and is economical. Ordinary RC relies on bars alone, cracks more, and may need a larger section for the same service limits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern codes treat partial prestressing through allowable tensile stress and crack-width limits rather than a single label. Bridge and precast industries use it to optimise girder depth, tendon count and camber. Research extends the idea to high-strength and fibre-reinforced concretes, where tension stiffening and crack spacing change. Search next for degree of prestressing, crack-width control in partially prestressed concrete, and strain-compatibility analysis of prestressed sections.
